topic: DeepSeek V4.1 Flash: what the best-hacking-model eval actually measured, and what transfers to your hardware
title: DeepSeek V4.1 Flash: the Hacking Crown Your Download Doesn't Get
description:
DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, AI Hacking Race benchmark, DGX Spark local inference.
The headlines crowned DeepSeek V4.1 Flash the best hacking model after it verified code execution on every vulnerable target for $4.65. The receipt tells a narrower story: 266.2 million of 268.3 million input tokens were provider cache hits billed cheaper, and the closest public local run is a 4x DGX Spark cluster at 77.2 tok/s peak, not one GPU. The weights are MIT-licensed and genuinely the same brain; the serving stack that made the score cheap is not in the download.
You'll learn what the benchmark actually measured, why mixture-of-experts speed still costs giant-model memory, and what transfers to your hardware tonight.
(Narration is AI-generated.)

The crown is real. The copy is not.

Everyone read the score. Nobody read the receipt.
Same model, same weights, minus the caching.
narration_full: You're crowning the wrong winner. You've got a gaming PC, and you saw the headline. An open-weights model swept a hacking benchmark. The win is real. The benchmark hands an agent a low-privilege account and one shell. A run only counts when the target executes a command and returns fresh proof. DeepSeek's V four point one Flash hacked every vulnerable target. Every patched one held. The whole sweep cost four dollars and sixty-five cents. The leaderboard itself warns it is not a general model ranking. Now read the receipt. Two hundred sixty-six million of the two hundred sixty-eight million input tokens were cache hits. A cache hit is input the provider already processed once, re-billed cheaper. That discount is a serving-stack trick. The weights play no part in it. The model is a mixture of experts, a company of specialists with a receptionist who wakes only the few each word needs. Speed comes from the few that wake. Memory comes from the whole company, because any specialist could be next. The receptionist re-picks for every word, so picture hundreds of small wake-ups per sentence. The closest public local run is four DGX Spark boxes wired as one, the model split across them. Peak speed: seventy-seven point two tokens per second. One consumer GPU cannot shelve the full weight set at all. The extra memory tables sit on disk, exiled, just to make room. Locally the currencies are memory and tokens per second. The weights are yours under an M I T license, free to download tonight, free to use commercially. The brain in that benchmark is the same brain you would get. The building around it stays behind: the caching, the serving stack, the discount. The honest claim is smaller than the headline. The benchmark crowned a model plus its serving stack. Your download is the same brain, minus the caching.

analogy.vehicle: A company of specialists with a receptionist at the front desk who wakes only the few each word needs.
analogy.mapping: The specialists are the experts inside the mixture-of-experts model and the receptionist is the router: per-word speed comes from the few that wake, while the memory bill comes from the whole company, because any specialist could be called next.
analogy.limit: The receptionist re-picks for every single word, so it is hundreds of small wake-ups per sentence, not one hand-off per question.

notes_for_review: Three-number cap spent on: $4.65 (spoken + on screen in s2), 266.2M of 268.3M cache hits (spoken + on screen in s3), and 77.2 tok/s (spoken only in s5, appears in no on_screen_text). Deliberately dropped per the cap: 11 of 11, 552B, 196B, 8B/16B, 890 bytes per token; they surface only qualitatively ('every vulnerable target', 'the full weight set', 'the extra memory tables'). Hedging: the 4x DGX Spark / 77.2 tok/s figure is one reviewer's forum deployment (medium confidence), so narration calls it 'the closest public local run', per the brief's Notes; Enclave's own 'not a general model ranking' warning is included as the honest catch. Analogy (receptionist) states its limit in s4. Check TTS rendering of 'M I T' (spelled for letter-by-letter reading) and 'V four point one'. Single wry beat is 'exiled' in s5, on the mechanism, not in hook or payoff. No 'Not X, but Y' construction used; the antithesis lives in the payoff's plain contrast instead.
